claims.text: An actively learned machine-learning potential can substantially reduce the cost of obtaining fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties.
The ML potential can accurately represent the free-energy landscapes of both solid and liquid states.
The ML framework can retain vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling.
The method can be applied to elemental, binary, and multicomponent high-entropy alloys near their fusion temperatures.
Iterative active learning with sparse ab initio data can build an accurate surrogate for the free energies of both solid and liquid states.
Structural descriptors in the ML potential can capture vibrational effects, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling.
Capturing those effects will make the surrogate faithful to the free-energy landscapes of both phases.
Iterative refinement of an ML surrogate can minimize the number of costly ab initio evaluations while retaining sufficient fidelity across states and compositions.
The framework may reduce computational cost by an order of magnitude relative to full ab initio molecular dynamics.
For elemental and binary systems, the framework can maintain free-energy accuracy comparable to TOR-TILD.
The framework can extend fusion free-energy calculations to high-entropy systems.
Explicit ab initio free-energy calculations based on molecular dynamics are accurate but computationally expensive.
TOR-TILD is computationally expensive, especially for multicomponent alloys.
The method is expected to cover compositions ranging from pure elements to high-entropy alloys.
The method is expected to operate from just below the fusion point through complete melting.
Prior elemental and binary results support the use of ML surrogates for this fusion free-energy task.
Scaling and fidelity in highly multicomponent high-entropy systems remain unverified.
A deviation greater than 5% in phase free energies or a cost reduction smaller than tenfold relative to ab initio MD would falsify the hypothesis.
